meta.title: Workforce, skilled trades and training, 17 days of posts
meta.subject: workforce development and skilled-trades policy in Texas — the Governor's Texas Jobs Council, career and technical education, apprenticeships and trades licensure, TSTC and community college funding, JET grants, workforce programs in juvenile justice, and state funding for academic programs like MATHCOUNTS
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 17, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas workforce, skilled trades and training policy, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Short-term credentials fill jobs
lanes.description: Fast, employer-aligned short-term programs, such as Workforce Pell at community colleges, give Texans a quick path to high-wage, in-demand jobs without a four-year degree.

lanes.label: Booming economy needs skilled workforce
lanes.description: Texas' economic and energy dominance depends on state investment in training workers for industries like oil and gas, manufacturing and data centers.

lanes.label: CTE builds school-to-career pathways
lanes.description: Career and technical education in Texas ISDs and local college partnerships prepare students for trades and careers, led by dedicated educators and employer sponsors.

lanes.label: Student aid needs fraud oversight
lanes.description: Cases of student aid fraud and wasteful education spending show that state and federal workforce and college funding needs tighter accountability.

lanes.label: Workforce data used for immigration enforcement
lanes.description: Texas workforce and labor records are being opened to ICE and other enforcement, raising privacy and labor-supply concerns for immigrant workers.

lanes.label: Abbott's tech push as globalist plot
lanes.description: Abbott's focus on crypto, data centers and human capital is framed as part of a global economic reset, not real opportunity for Texas workers.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Lubbock-Cooper ISD
posts.text:
It is with great sadness that we share the passing of Lubbock-Cooper ISD Director of Career and Technical Education Dr. Sarah Allen.

Dr. Allen served the LCP family for 15 years as a classroom teacher, Director of CTE, and true champion for all Pirates and Patriots. She established the district's Culinary Arts program, starting with an after-school cooking club and developing it into one of the most robust and respected school culinary programs in Texas. As Director of CTE, she brought that same passion and determination to every career program across the district, constantly seeking new opportunities, grants, partnerships, and innovative ideas to ensure our students had access to the very best programs and opportunities available. She was always looking for ways to move our CTE programs forward, keep them current and cutting-edge, and prepare our students for success beyond the classroom. She was honored as a National Teacher of the Month in 2021 and named the Texas Family and Consumer Science Teacher of the Year in 2024, among a multitude of other career accolades.

Beyond her impressive achievements as an educator, Dr. Allen was a deeply cherished friend and colleague, and an inspiration and cheerleader for all students. She opened doors for Lubbock-Cooper students and staff, loved them, advocated for them, and introduced them to opportunities they may not have even known existed without her guidance and encouragement. Our world has been made tremendously better because Sarah Allen was a part of it.

Services for Dr. Allen will be held at 10:00 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, at Indiana Avenue Baptist Church.

Our thoughts and prayers are with Dr. Allen's family, our fellow members of the LCP family, and the hundreds of staff, students, and families whose lives she touched.

posts.name: Owen Gregorian
posts.text:
Former Texas Professor Gets Over Six Years for $921K Student Aid Fraud Scheme | Matt Vespa, Townhall

A 43-year-old man living in Richmond, TX, will serve time in federal prison for orchestrating a years-long scheme involving fraudulent student financial aid applications and the misuse of victims’ identities.

Emmanuel Olugbaike Finnih is originally from Nigeria and later became a naturalized U.S. citizen. He was also formerly an adjunct professor at Texas Southern University.

Finnih pleaded guilty on March 20 to theft of government funds, fraud, unlawful use or transfer of identity documents, and aggravated identity theft.

U.S. District Judge Andrew Hanen ordered Finnih to serve 78 months in federal prison to be immediately followed by three years of supervised release. At the hearing, the court heard how Finnih used false identities, transcripts, UPS boxes, and bank accounts to carry out the scheme, leaving victims with student loan debt that damaged their credit and hindered legitimate school enrollment.

“Higher education costs are already skyrocketing out of control, and it’s scammers like Finnih who make it worse, more expensive, and financially damaging for everyone,” said U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz. “This fraudster will now suffer the consequences of his manipulative, deceitful, un-American crimes.”

For about five years, Finnih submitted more than 100 fraudulent financial aid applications to the Department of Education using the identities of numerous straw students at colleges and universities across Texas.

“I am proud of the work of OIG Special Agents and our law enforcement partners for shutting down another student aid fraud ring and holding Mr. Finnih accountable for his criminal actions,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Scott Wingle of the U.S. Department of Education Office of Inspector General’s Central Regional Office. “We will continue to aggressively pursue those who misappropriate education funds for their own selfish purposes. America’s students and taxpayers deserve nothing less.”

He used other individuals’ personal identifying information to prepare, submit, and sign fraudulent financial aid applications and master promissory notes in their names. He also used mailing addresses, phone numbers, and email accounts he controlled to receive communications from the Department of Education and the schools.

Finnih then obtained financial aid refunds through electronic transfers, checks, and prepaid debit cards sent to addresses or bank accounts he controlled.

As part of his plea, Finnih admitted repeatedly using the personal identifying information of two victims over several years to fraudulently obtain federal financial aid.

Authorities also discovered Finnih possessed false identity documents, including temporary driver permits and identification cards, that he intended to unlawfully use or transfer as part of the scheme.

The fraud left some victims with tens of thousands of dollars in student loans fraudulently placed in their names, significantly affecting their credit.

The court also heard how Finnih would often masculinize the names of female straw students while continuing to use their correct Social Security numbers and dates of birth. This allowed him to pose as the straw students more easily and further the scheme.

In at least one instance, Finnih called a local community college and attempted to have financial aid payments unfrozen after the school flagged fraudulent transcripts associated with one of the straw students.

Finnih submitted fraudulent aid applications seeking over $1.3 million in grants and loans, of which $921,189.08 was disbursed.

Finnih was permitted to remain on bond and voluntarily surrender to a Federal Bureau of Prisons facility to be determined in the near future.

Department of Education – OIG investigated with assistance from the Lone Star College Police Department, U.S. Marshals Service and U.S. Postal Inspection Service. Assistant U.S. Attorney Brad R. Gray prosecuted the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division, which is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within federal benefit programs.
